slides.title: The Accounting Equation
slides.text:
The Accounting Equation
01
Every transaction, no matter how complex, keeps this equation in balance.
ASSETS = LIABILITIES + EQUITY
What the business owns
cash, inventory, equipment, buildings
What the business owes
loans, accounts payable, unearned revenue
The owner's residual claim
capital invested + retained earnings
Worked Example — Northstar Bike Co.
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 3
Transaction | Assets | Liabilities | Equity
Alex invests $5,000 cash to start the business | +$5,000 cash | $0 | +$5,000 capital
Buys a $1,200 bike repair stand on credit | +$1,200 equipment | +$1,200 payable | $0
Earns $300 cash from bike sales | +$300 cash | $0 | +$300 revenue

slides.title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
slides.text:
Double-Entry Bookkeeping
02
Every transaction touches at least two accounts — total debits always equal total credits.
Which side increases an account?
Memory tip: "DEAD" accounts (Dividends, Expenses, Assets, Draws) increase with debits — everything else increases with credits.
Worked Example — Journal Entry
Northstar Bike Co. pays $1,200 cash to buy a new repair stand.
Equipment (an asset) goes up, so it's debited. Cash (also an asset) goes down, so it's
credited. Total debits ($1,200) = total credits ($1,200).
Balance check: Debits $1,200 = Credits $1,200 ✓
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 4
Account Type | Debit | Credit
Assets | Increase | Decrease
Expenses | Increase | Decrease
Liabilities | Decrease | Increase
Equity | Decrease | Increase
Revenue | Decrease | Increase
Account | Debit | Credit
Equipment (Asset) | $1,200
Cash (Asset) | $1,200

slides.title: The Three Core Financial Statements
slides.text:
The Three Core Financial Statements
03
Together, they answer: what do we own, how did we perform, and where did the cash go?
1
Balance Sheet
A snapshot at one point in time
Assets = Liabilities + Equity
“What do we own and owe today?”
2
Income Statement
Performance over a period
Revenue − Expenses = Net Income
“Did we make a profit this year?”
3
Cash Flow Statement
Cash movement over a period
Operating + Investing + Financing
“Where did our cash actually go?”
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 5

slides.title: Example: The Balance Sheet
slides.text:
Example: The Balance Sheet
03a
Northstar Bike Co. — as of December 31, 2025
ASSETS
Cash $8,500
Accounts Receivable $1,200
Inventory (bikes & parts) $2,300
Repair & Shop Equipment $14,000
Less: Accumulated Depreciation ($2,000)
Total Assets $24,000
Cash + AR + Inventory + Equipment (net) = 8,500 + 1,200 + 2,300 + 12,000
LIABILITIES & EQUITY
Accounts Payable $1,800
Bank Loan (long-term) $6,200
Owner's Capital $14,000
Retained Earnings $2,000
Total Liabilities + Equity $24,000
Balance check: Assets $24,000 = Liabilities $8,000 + Equity $16,000 ✓
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 6

slides.title: Example: The Income Statement
slides.text:
Example: The Income Statement
03b
Northstar Bike Co. — Year Ended December 31, 2025
Sales Revenue $52,000
Less: Cost of Goods Sold ($21,000)
Gross Profit $31,000
Operating Expenses:
Wages ($14,000)
Rent ($6,000)
Depreciation ($2,000)
Utilities & Other ($1,500)
Operating Income $7,500
Less: Interest Expense ($500)
NET INCOME $7,000
Reading it top to bottom
Gross Profit shows what's left after making the product
Operating Income shows profit from core business activity
Net Income is the “bottom line” — what the owner actually earns
Net Income flows into Retained Earnings on the balance sheet
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 7

Example: The Cash Flow Statement
03c
Northstar Bike Co. — Year Ended December 31, 2025. Net income doesn't equal cash — this statement shows why.
Operating Activities
Investing Activities
Purchase of Equipment ($3,000)
Net Cash from Investing ($3,000)
Financing Activities
Net Cash from Financing ($200)
Net Change in Cash: $9,200 − $3,000 − $200 = +$6,000
Net Income | $7,000
+ Depreciation (non-cash) | $2,000
+ Decrease in Inventory | $500
− Increase in Receivables | ($300)
Net Cash from Operations | $9,200
Owner Contribution | $1,000
Loan Repayment | ($1,200)

slides.title: Accrual vs. Cash Basis Accounting
slides.text:
Accrual vs. Cash Basis Accounting
04
The difference is timing: when do you record revenue and expenses?
Cash Basis
Record revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid.
Simple; used by small businesses and freelancers
Accrual Basis
Record revenue when earned and expenses when incurred — regardless of when cash moves.
Required under GAAP for most companies; matches revenue to the period it was earned
Worked Example
Northstar Bike Co. completes a custom bike build on December 28, 2025 and invoices the client $2,000. The client pays on January 15, 2026.
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 9
Cash Basis | Accrual Basis
Revenue recorded in... | January 2026 (when paid) | December 2025 (when earned)

slides.title: Depreciation
slides.text:
Depreciation
05
Spreading the cost of a long-term asset over the years it's used, instead of expensing it all at once.
Straight-Line Formula
Annual Depreciation =
(Cost − Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life
Example: Delivery Van (Northstar Bike Co.)
$32,000
Cost
$2,000
Salvage Value
5 years
Useful Life
($32,000 − $2,000) ÷ 5 = $6,000 per year
5-Year Depreciation Schedule
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 10
Year | Depreciation Expense | Accumulated Depreciation | Book Value (End of Year)

2 | $6,000 | $12,000 | $20,000
3 | $6,000 | $18,000 | $14,000

slides.title: Key Financial Ratios
slides.text:
Key Financial Ratios
06
Ratios turn raw statement numbers into signals about liquidity, profitability, and leverage.
Current Ratio
Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
Liquidity — can we cover short-term bills?
Gross Margin
Gross Profit ÷ Revenue
Profitability — how efficient is production?
Net Margin
Net Income ÷ Revenue
Profitability — what share of sales is profit?
Debt-to-Equity
Total Liabilities ÷ Total Equity
Leverage — how much financing is debt?
Northstar Bike Co. — Ratios in Action
Current Ratio: $12,000 ÷ $8,000 = 1.5
Debt-to-Equity: $8,000 ÷ $16,000 = 0.5
A current ratio above 1.0 and modest debt-to-equity both signal a financially healthy bike shop.
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 11

slides.title: Core GAAP Principles
slides.text:
Core GAAP Principles
06b
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles keep financial statements consistent and comparable.
1
Revenue Recognition
Recognize revenue when it's earned, not necessarily when cash is received.
2
Matching Principle
Match expenses to the revenue they helped generate, in the same period.
3
Consistency
Use the same accounting methods period to period so results are comparable.
4
Conservatism
When in doubt, record losses early and gains only when they're realized.
5
Going Concern
Assume the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future.
6
Materiality
Only items large enough to influence a decision need precise, separate treatment.
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 12

slides.title: Test Your Knowledge
slides.text:
Test Your Knowledge
QUICK CHECK
Discuss each question with a partner before checking the answer key (see speaker notes).
Q1
Which statement reports revenue and expenses over a period of time?
A. Balance Sheet
B. Income Statement
C. Cash Flow Statement
D. Trial Balance
Q2
Northstar Bike Co. buys a repair stand with cash. What happens to total assets?
A. Increase
B. Decrease
C. No change — one asset for another
D. Cannot be determined
Q3
Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when it is...
A. Invoiced to the customer
B. Earned, regardless of cash timing
C. Received in cash
D. Approved at year-end
Q4
Depreciation expense is best described as...
A. Cash paid for a new asset
B. Allocating an asset's cost over its useful life
C. A liability owed to the bank
D. A reduction in liabilities
Q5
Current Assets $12,000 ÷ Current Liabilities $8,000. What does the result tell us?
A. 0.67 — weak liquidity
B. 1.5 — can cover short-term obligations comfortably
C. 1.5 — dangerously over-leveraged
D. 8.0 — holding too much cash
DISCUSS
Northstar Bike Co. has strong net income but low
cash on hand. How is that possible — and which
statement would you check first to find out?
Financial Accounting Fundamentals 13
